narrative:
The model estimates you have a 47% chance of failing your final year, which is high enough that the school requires you to take remedial courses to strengthen your chances of graduating.

The prediction is driven mainly by three aspects of your situation. By far the strongest factor is that you have already failed one class in the past. While students who passed had zero previous failures on average, your history of one failure strongly pulled the model toward expecting you to struggle again. This single piece of information had the greatest influence on the outcome.

Two other factors worked in your favor but were not strong enough to overcome the past failure. Your family size of three or fewer members is more common among students who succeed than those who fail, and this gave a modest push toward passing. Similarly, the amount of time you spend studying each week (2–5 hours) is actually typical of many students who ultimately pass, which also nudged the prediction slightly in a positive direction.

To improve, focus first on breaking the pattern of past failure. Speak with your teachers about targeted support in the subjects that caused difficulty before, and consider increasing your weekly study time beyond the 2–5 hours you currently spend. Small, consistent changes in these areas can meaningfully raise your chances of passing.
